claim: Antibody-mediated neutrophil depletion reduced disease severity in a mouse model of genital HSV-2 infection.
source: In a mouse model of genital herpes simplex virus-2 (HSV-2) infection, which results in severe genital inflammation, antibody-mediated neutrophil depletion reduced disease.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that antibody-mediated neutrophil depletion reduced disease in the HSV-2 infection model, and this is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: HSV-2 infection results in severe genital inflammation in mice.
source: In a mouse model of genital herpes simplex virus-2 (HSV-2) infection, which results in severe genital inflammation, antibody-mediated neutrophil depletion reduced disease.
evidence: The manuscript describes the HSV-2 infection model as resulting in severe genital inflammation, supported by inflammation scores and histological data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Comparative single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis demonstrated sustained expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) after HSV-2 infection primarily within the neutrophil population.
source: Comparative single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis of vaginal cells against a model of genital HSV-1 infection, which results in mild inflammation, demonstrated sustained expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) only after HSV-2 infection primarily within the neutrophil population.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by scRNA-seq data presented in Figure 3, showing ISG expression patterns in neutrophil clusters.

claim: HSV-1 genital infection results in mild inflammation compared to HSV-2.
source: Comparative single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis of vaginal cells against a model of genital HSV-1 infection, which results in mild inflammation, demonstrated sustained expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) only after HSV-2 infection primarily within the neutrophil population.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that HSV-1 infection results in mild inflammation, supported by inflammation scores in Figure 2A showing significantly lower disease scores for HSV-1 compared to HSV-2.

claim: Therapeutic blockade of IFNα/β receptor 1 (IFNAR1) decreased HSV-2 genital disease severity.
source: Both therapeutic blockade of IFNα/β receptor 1 (IFNAR1) and genetic deletion of IFNAR1 in neutrophils concomitantly decreased HSV-2 genital disease severity and vaginal IL-18 levels.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data in Figure 4A showing reduced inflammation scores after therapeutic IFNAR1 blockade.

claim: Genetic deletion of IFNAR1 in neutrophils decreased HSV-2 genital disease severity.
source: Both therapeutic blockade of IFNα/β receptor 1 (IFNAR1) and genetic deletion of IFNAR1 in neutrophils concomitantly decreased HSV-2 genital disease severity and vaginal IL-18 levels.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data in Figure 5C showing reduced inflammation scores in IFNAR1 CKO mice.

claim: Therapeutic blockade of IFNAR1 decreased vaginal IL-18 levels during HSV-2 infection.
source: Both therapeutic blockade of IFNα/β receptor 1 (IFNAR1) and genetic deletion of IFNAR1 in neutrophils concomitantly decreased HSV-2 genital disease severity and vaginal IL-18 levels.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data in Figure 6B showing reduced IL-18 levels after therapeutic IFNAR1 blockade.

claim: Genetic deletion of IFNAR1 in neutrophils decreased vaginal IL-18 levels during HSV-2 infection.
source: Both therapeutic blockade of IFNα/β receptor 1 (IFNAR1) and genetic deletion of IFNAR1 in neutrophils concomitantly decreased HSV-2 genital disease severity and vaginal IL-18 levels.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data in Figure 6C showing reduced IL-18 levels in IFNAR1 CKO mice.

claim: Therapeutic neutralization of IL-18 diminished genital inflammation during HSV-2 infection.
source: Therapeutic neutralization of IL-18 also diminished genital inflammation, indicating an important role for this cytokine in promoting neutrophil-dependent immunopathology.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data in Figure 6D showing reduced inflammation scores after IL-18 neutralization.

claim: Sustained type I interferon signaling is a driver of pathogenic neutrophil responses during HSV-2 infection.
source: Our study reveals that sustained type I interferon (IFN) signaling is a driver of pathogenic neutrophil responses and identifies IL-18 as a novel component of disease during genital HSV-2 infection.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this conclusion, which is supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including scRNA-seq data, IFNAR1 blockade experiments, and neutrophil-specific IFNAR1 deletion.

claim: IL-18 is a novel component of disease during genital HSV-2 infection.
source: Our study reveals that sustained type I interferon (IFN) signaling is a driver of pathogenic neutrophil responses and identifies IL-18 as a novel component of disease during genital HSV-2 infection.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data showing IL-18 levels correlate with disease and IL-18 neutralization reduces inflammation.

claim: Neutrophils are the most abundant leukocytes in circulation in humans.
source: In humans, they are the most abundant leukocytes in circulation and are often among the first wave of immune cells responding to pathogen invasion.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction without specific citation, representing general scientific consensus.

claim: Neutrophils are often among the first wave of immune cells responding to pathogen invasion.
source: In humans, they are the most abundant leukocytes in circulation and are often among the first wave of immune cells responding to pathogen invasion.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction, representing general scientific consensus about neutrophil biology.

claim: Neutrophils are largely protective during bacterial or fungal infections, including sexually transmitted infections.
source: In the context of bacterial or fungal infections, including those that are sexually transmitted, neutrophils are largely protective and can help eliminate pathogens through a variety of effector functions, including phagocytosis, production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), neutrophil extracellular traps (NET) and protease release, and cytokine and chemokine secretion (Mayadas et al., 2014; Pham, 2006; Tecchio et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Mayadas et al., 2014; Pham, 2006; Tecchio et al., 2014).

claim: Neutrophils can eliminate pathogens through phagocytosis, production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), neutrophil extracellular traps (NET) and protease release, and cytokine and chemokine secretion.
source: In the context of bacterial or fungal infections, including those that are sexually transmitted, neutrophils are largely protective and can help eliminate pathogens through a variety of effector functions, including phagocytosis, production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), neutrophil extracellular traps (NET) and protease release, and cytokine and chemokine secretion (Mayadas et al., 2014; Pham, 2006; Tecchio et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Mayadas et al., 2014; Pham, 2006; Tecchio et al., 2014).

claim: The role of neutrophils during viral infection is less clear than during bacterial or fungal infections.
source: In contrast, the role of neutrophils during viral infection is less clear (Galani and Andreakos, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Galani and Andreakos, 2015.

claim: Neutrophils have been reported to neutralize several viruses and display protective qualities in vivo.
source: While neutrophils have been reported to neutralize several viruses and display protective qualities in vivo (Akk et al., 2016; Jenne et al., 2013; Saitoh et al., 2012; Tate et al., 2009; Tate et al., 2011), they have also been associated with tissue damage, loss of viral control, and increased mortality (Bai et al., 2010; Brandes et al., 2013; Kulkarni et al., 2019; Narasaraju et al., 2011; Vidy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Akk et al., 2016; Jenne et al., 2013; Saitoh et al., 2012; Tate et al., 2009; Tate et al., 2011).

claim: Neutrophils have been associated with tissue damage, loss of viral control, and increased mortality during viral infections.
source: While neutrophils have been reported to neutralize several viruses and display protective qualities in vivo (Akk et al., 2016; Jenne et al., 2013; Saitoh et al., 2012; Tate et al., 2009; Tate et al., 2011), they have also been associated with tissue damage, loss of viral control, and increased mortality (Bai et al., 2010; Brandes et al., 2013; Kulkarni et al., 2019; Narasaraju et al., 2011; Vidy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Bai et al., 2010; Brandes et al., 2013; Kulkarni et al., 2019; Narasaraju et al., 2011; Vidy et al., 2016).

claim: Type I IFNs can enhance recruitment of neutrophils to sites of infection.
source: Type I IFNs can enhance recruitment of neutrophils to sites of infection, regulate neutrophil function, and drive immunopathology after infection by different classes of pathogens, including Plasmodium spp., Candida spp., and Pseudomonas spp. (Majer et al., 2012; Pylaeva et al., 2019; Rocha et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Majer et al., 2012; Pylaeva et al., 2019; Rocha et al., 2015).

claim: Type I IFNs can regulate neutrophil function.
source: Type I IFNs can enhance recruitment of neutrophils to sites of infection, regulate neutrophil function, and drive immunopathology after infection by different classes of pathogens, including Plasmodium spp., Candida spp., and Pseudomonas spp. (Majer et al., 2012; Pylaeva et al., 2019; Rocha et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Majer et al., 2012; Pylaeva et al., 2019; Rocha et al., 2015).

claim: Type I IFNs can drive immunopathology after infection by Plasmodium spp., Candida spp., and Pseudomonas spp.
source: Type I IFNs can enhance recruitment of neutrophils to sites of infection, regulate neutrophil function, and drive immunopathology after infection by different classes of pathogens, including Plasmodium spp., Candida spp., and Pseudomonas spp. (Majer et al., 2012; Pylaeva et al., 2019; Rocha et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Majer et al., 2012; Pylaeva et al., 2019; Rocha et al., 2015).

claim: Type I IFNs can inhibit neutrophil recruitment to the ganglia by suppressing chemokine expression after herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection.
source: However, type I IFNs can also inhibit neutrophil recruitment to the ganglia by suppressing chemokine expression after herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection (Stock et al., 2014), suggesting that the interplay of IFNs and neutrophil activity may be dependent on tissue type and the pathogen.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stock et al., 2014.

claim: The interplay of IFNs and neutrophil activity may be dependent on tissue type and the pathogen.
source: However, type I IFNs can also inhibit neutrophil recruitment to the ganglia by suppressing chemokine expression after herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection (Stock et al., 2014), suggesting that the interplay of IFNs and neutrophil activity may be dependent on tissue type and the pathogen.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited work (Stock et al., 2014) and the broader context of IFN-neutrophil interactions.

claim: Type I IFNs can promote expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) and pro-inflammatory cytokines in neutrophils.
source: Type I IFNs can promote expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) and pro-inflammatory cytokines in neutrophils, suggesting a potential role for them in driving immunopathology (Galani et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Galani et al., 2017.

claim: IFNAR signaling appears to suppress neutrophil-dependent killing of parasites during Leishmania infection.
source: During Leishmania infection, however, IFNAR signaling appears to suppress neutrophil-dependent killing of parasites (Xin et al., 2010), which emphasizes the complexity of IFN-mediated neutrophil responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Xin et al., 2010.

claim: Genital herpes affects over 400 million people worldwide.
source: Genital herpes is a chronic, sexually transmitted infection that affects over 400 million people worldwide (World Health Organization, 2007) and can be caused by two members of the alphaherpesvirus family, HSV-2 or the related HSV-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to World Health Organization, 2007.

claim: Genital herpes can be caused by HSV-2 or HSV-1.
source: Genital herpes is a chronic, sexually transmitted infection that affects over 400 million people worldwide (World Health Organization, 2007) and can be caused by two members of the alphaherpesvirus family, HSV-2 or the related HSV-1.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about genital herpes etiology.

claim: Genital herpes is characterized by recurrent episodes of inflammation and ulceration.
source: Genital herpes is characterized by recurrent episodes of inflammation and ulceration, and the factors that drive disease are unclear.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about genital herpes clinical presentation.

claim: In humans, ulcer formation is associated with suboptimal viral control and spread during episodes of reactivation.
source: In humans, ulcer formation is associated with suboptimal viral control and spread during episodes of reactivation (Roychoudhury et al., 2020; Schiffer and Corey, 2013; Schiffer et al., 2013), while in mouse models, severity of disease often correlates with susceptibility to infection and the level of viral replication in the genital mucosa (Gopinath et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Roychoudhury et al., 2020; Schiffer and Corey, 2013; Schiffer et al., 2013).

claim: In mouse models, severity of disease often correlates with susceptibility to infection and the level of viral replication in the genital mucosa.
source: In humans, ulcer formation is associated with suboptimal viral control and spread during episodes of reactivation (Roychoudhury et al., 2020; Schiffer and Corey, 2013; Schiffer et al., 2013), while in mouse models, severity of disease often correlates with susceptibility to infection and the level of viral replication in the genital mucosa (Gopinath et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gopinath et al., 2018.

claim: Neutrophil infiltration into sites of active HSV-2 ulcers has been reported in humans.
source: Neutrophil infiltration into sites of active HSV-2 ulcers has also been reported in humans (Boddingius et al., 1987), but whether these cells are helpful or harmful during HSV infection is unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Boddingius et al., 1987.

claim: Neutrophils have been associated with tissue damage after multiple routes of HSV-1 infection.
source: While neutrophils have been associated with tissue damage after multiple routes of HSV-1 infection (Divito and Hendricks, 2008; Khoury-Hanold et al., 2016; Rao and Suvas, 2019; Thomas et al., 1997), a protective role for neutrophils after genital HSV-2 infection has also been reported (Milligan, 1999; Milligan et al., 2001), although the use of non-specific depletion antibodies has muddled the respective contribution of neutrophils and other innate immune cells such as monocytes, which are known to be antiviral (Iijima et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Divito and Hendricks, 2008; Khoury-Hanold et al., 2016; Rao and Suvas, 2019; Thomas et al., 1997).

claim: A protective role for neutrophils after genital HSV-2 infection has been reported.
source: While neutrophils have been associated with tissue damage after multiple routes of HSV-1 infection (Divito and Hendricks, 2008; Khoury-Hanold et al., 2016; Rao and Suvas, 2019; Thomas et al., 1997), a protective role for neutrophils after genital HSV-2 infection has also been reported (Milligan, 1999; Milligan et al., 2001), although the use of non-specific depletion antibodies has muddled the respective contribution of neutrophils and other innate immune cells such as monocytes, which are known to be antiviral (Iijima et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Milligan, 1999; Milligan et al., 2001).

claim: Monocytes are known to be antiviral during HSV infection.
source: While neutrophils have been associated with tissue damage after multiple routes of HSV-1 infection (Divito and Hendricks, 2008; Khoury-Hanold et al., 2016; Rao and Suvas, 2019; Thomas et al., 1997), a protective role for neutrophils after genital HSV-2 infection has also been reported (Milligan, 1999; Milligan et al., 2001), although the use of non-specific depletion antibodies has muddled the respective contribution of neutrophils and other innate immune cells such as monocytes, which are known to be antiviral (Iijima et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Iijima et al., 2011.

claim: Increased neutrophil recruitment to the HSV-2-infected vaginal epithelial barrier resulted in greater epithelial cell death.
source: Furthermore, increased neutrophil recruitment to the HSV-2-infected vaginal epithelial barrier resulted in greater epithelial cell death, suggesting that neutrophil responses may indeed be pathogenic (Krzyzowska et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krzyzowska et al., 2014.

claim: Neutrophils were effectively reduced up to 6 days post-infection in the vagina after anti-Ly6G antibody treatment.
source: Neutrophils were effectively reduced up to 6 days post-infection (d.p.i.) in the vagina (Figure 1A) and the blood (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neutrophils were effectively reduced up to 6 days post-infection in the blood after anti-Ly6G antibody treatment.
source: Neutrophils were effectively reduced up to 6 days post-infection (d.p.i.) in the vagina (Figure 1A) and the blood (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Progression of disease in neutrophil-depleted mice was significantly slower compared to controls during HSV-2 infection.
source: Over time, progression of disease in the neutrophil-depleted mice was significantly slower compared to the controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by inflammation score data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: As late as 7 d.p.i., a proportion of the neutrophil-depleted group remained uninflamed, in contrast to the isotype control group in which all mice displayed signs of inflammation.
source: Remarkably, as late as 7 d.p.i., a proportion of the neutrophil-depleted group remained uninflamed, in contrast to the isotype control group in which all mice displayed signs of inflammation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by inflammation score data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At 6 d.p.i., epithelial denuding and damage was apparent in the isotype control-treated mice.
source: At 6 d.p.i., epithelial denuding and damage was apparent in the isotype control-treated mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Only a limited amount of epithelial destruction was observed in neutrophil-depleted mice at 6 d.p.i.
source: In contrast, only a limited amount of epithelial destruction was observed in neutrophil-depleted mice, with less cellular infiltrates at sites of damage and in the lumen (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Differences in genital inflammation and mucosal damage were largely independent of changes in viral control in the absence of neutrophils.
source: Unexpectedly, differences in genital inflammation and mucosal damage were largely independent of changes in viral control in the absence of neutrophils, as viral shedding into the vaginal lumen (Figure 1D) and viral control in the tissue parenchyma (Figure 1E) were similar between the two groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: Viral shedding into the vaginal lumen was similar between neutrophil-depleted and control groups.
source: Unexpectedly, differences in genital inflammation and mucosal damage were largely independent of changes in viral control in the absence of neutrophils, as viral shedding into the vaginal lumen (Figure 1D) and viral control in the tissue parenchyma (Figure 1E) were similar between the two groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Viral control in the tissue parenchyma was similar between neutrophil-depleted and control groups.
source: Unexpectedly, differences in genital inflammation and mucosal damage were largely independent of changes in viral control in the absence of neutrophils, as viral shedding into the vaginal lumen (Figure 1D) and viral control in the tissue parenchyma (Figure 1E) were similar between the two groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Disease severity was decreased in neutrophil-depleted mice despite a slight delay in the resolution of viral replication at 5 d.p.i.
source: Indeed, disease severity was decreased in neutrophil-depleted mice despite a slight delay in the resolution of viral replication at 5 d.p.i. (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by inflammation score and viral titer data shown in Figures 1B and 1D.

claim: In vitro stimulation of neutrophils with HSV-2 resulted in the enlargement of cell nuclei and the characteristic expulsion of DNA coated in citrullinated histones.
source: In vitro stimulation of neutrophils with HSV-2 resulted in the enlargement of cell nuclei and the characteristic expulsion of DNA coated in citrullinated histones, which is a key characteristic of NETs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: HSV-2 infection of PAD4 CKO mice and their littermate controls demonstrated minimal impact on genital inflammation.
source: HSV-2 infection of these mice and their littermate controls demonstrated minimal impact on genital inflammation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B) or viral replication (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C) in the genital mucosa.
evidence: This claim is supported by inflammation score data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: HSV-2 infection of PAD4 CKO mice and their littermate controls demonstrated minimal impact on viral replication.
source: HSV-2 infection of these mice and their littermate controls demonstrated minimal impact on genital inflammation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B) or viral replication (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C) in the genital mucosa.
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: PAD4 expression in neutrophils and likely NET formation are not the mechanisms by which these cells mediate disease after HSV-2 infection.
source: Thus, our data show that PAD4 expression in neutrophils and likely NET formation are not the mechanisms by which these cells mediate disease after HSV-2 infection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing no effect of PAD4 deletion on disease severity.

claim: In vitro stimulation of neutrophils with HSV-2 led to an increase in ROS production compared to unstimulated cells.
source: We found that in vitro stimulation of neutrophils with HSV-2 led to an increase in ROS production compared to unstimulated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data measuring DCFDA fluorescence shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: HSV-2 infection of Ncf2 KO and heterozygous controls resulted in similar progression of disease.
source: HSV-2 infection of Ncf2 KO and heterozygous controls resulted in similar progression of disease (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B) and did not alter viral titer (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by inflammation score data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: HSV-2 infection of Ncf2 KO and heterozygous controls did not alter viral titer.
source: HSV-2 infection of Ncf2 KO and heterozygous controls resulted in similar progression of disease (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B) and did not alter viral titer (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: There was little difference in genital inflammation severity between the STIM1/2 DKO and Cre- controls.
source: As expected, there was little difference in genital inflammation severity between the STIM1/2 DKO and Cre- controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D) or viral titers (Figure 1—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by inflammation score data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: There was little difference in viral titers between the STIM1/2 DKO and Cre- controls.
source: As expected, there was little difference in genital inflammation severity between the STIM1/2 DKO and Cre- controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D) or viral titers (Figure 1—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4E.

claim: ROS production from neutrophils and other cell types play little role in driving genital inflammation after HSV-2 infection.
source: Together, our data show that ROS production from neutrophils and other cell types play little role in driving genital inflammation after HSV-2 infection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing no effect of Ncf2 or STIM1/2 deletion on disease severity.

claim: Inoculation with the same dose of HSV-1 and HSV-2 led to profound differences in genital inflammation.
source: Inoculation with the same dose of HSV-1 and HSV-2 led to profound differences in genital inflammation (Figure 2A) despite comparable levels of mucosal viral shedding throughout most days after infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Lee et al., 2020), although resolution of HSV-2 infection at 6 and 7 d.p.i. was delayed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by inflammation score data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: HSV-1 and HSV-2 infections resulted in comparable levels of mucosal viral shedding throughout most days after infection.
source: Inoculation with the same dose of HSV-1 and HSV-2 led to profound differences in genital inflammation (Figure 2A) despite comparable levels of mucosal viral shedding throughout most days after infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Lee et al., 2020), although resolution of HSV-2 infection at 6 and 7 d.p.i. was delayed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and cited work (Lee et al., 2020).

claim: Resolution of HSV-2 infection at 6 and 7 d.p.i. was delayed compared to HSV-1.
source: Inoculation with the same dose of HSV-1 and HSV-2 led to profound differences in genital inflammation (Figure 2A) despite comparable levels of mucosal viral shedding throughout most days after infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Lee et al., 2020), although resolution of HSV-2 infection at 6 and 7 d.p.i. was delayed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Magnitude of the neutrophil response in the vagina was similar between HSV-1- and HSV-2-infected mice during the course of acute mucosal infection.
source: Importantly, magnitude of the neutrophil response in the vagina was similar between HSV-1- and HSV-2-infected mice during the course of acute mucosal infection (Figure 2B), and neutrophils could be found infiltrating sites of both HSV-1- and HSV-2-infected epithelium (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Neutrophils could be found infiltrating sites of both HSV-1- and HSV-2-infected epithelium.
source: Importantly, magnitude of the neutrophil response in the vagina was similar between HSV-1- and HSV-2-infected mice during the course of acute mucosal infection (Figure 2B), and neutrophils could be found infiltrating sites of both HSV-1- and HSV-2-infected epithelium (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Antibody-mediated depletion of neutrophils prior to inoculation with HSV-1 did not reduce the development of genital inflammation during the first 7 days after infection.
source: In contrast to HSV-2 infection, antibody-mediated depletion of neutrophils with anti-Ly6G antibody prior to inoculation with HSV-1 did not reduce the development of genital inflammation during the first 7 days after infection (Figure 2D) and had minimal impact on acute viral control (Figure 2D - Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by inflammation score data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Neutrophil depletion had minimal impact on acute viral control during HSV-1 infection.
source: In contrast to HSV-2 infection, antibody-mediated depletion of neutrophils with anti-Ly6G antibody prior to inoculation with HSV-1 did not reduce the development of genital inflammation during the first 7 days after infection (Figure 2D) and had minimal impact on acute viral control (Figure 2D - Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The regulation of the neutrophil response after HSV-1 or HSV-2 infection was distinct.
source: Together, our data suggests that the regulation of the neutrophil response after HSV-1 or HSV-2 infection was distinct, which may contribute to the differences in disease outcomes between these infections.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects of neutrophil depletion on HSV-1 vs HSV-2 disease outcomes.

claim: Analysis across 21,633 cells in all samples revealed 17 unique clusters in the vagina during HSV infection after filtering.
source: Analysis across 21,633 cells in all samples revealed 17 unique clusters in the vagina during HSV infection after filtering, including myeloid cells, lymphocytes, and epithelial cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Neutrophils were identified by expression of known cell markers such as S100a8 and Csf3r.
source: Neutrophils were identified by expression of known cell markers such as S100a8 and Csf3r (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In mock-infected animals, the vaginal neutrophil population was dominated by cluster 0.
source: In mock-infected animals, the vaginal neutrophil population was dominated by cluster 0, and upon infection, at least two additional neutrophil subsets, cluster 2 and cluster 5, were clearly present (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Upon infection, at least two additional neutrophil subsets, cluster 2 and cluster 5, were clearly present.
source: In mock-infected animals, the vaginal neutrophil population was dominated by cluster 0, and upon infection, at least two additional neutrophil subsets, cluster 2 and cluster 5, were clearly present (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In HSV-2-infected mice, the presence of cluster 0 was greatly reduced, and the bulk of the neutrophils was composed of cluster 2 and 5.
source: While HSV-1-infected mice retained all three subpopulations of neutrophils in the vagina at 5 d.p.i., in HSV-2-infected mice, the presence of cluster 0 was greatly reduced, and the bulk of the neutrophils was composed of cluster 2 and 5 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cluster 0 expressed low levels of genes associated with a type I IFN response, even in infected animals.
source: One major distinguishing characteristic between 'homeostatic' cluster 0 and 'infection' clusters 2 and 5 was the extent of ISG expression, in which cluster 0 expressed low levels of genes associated with a type I IFN response, even in infected animals, while clusters 2 and 5 expressed high levels of these genes (Figure 3D; Liberzon et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D and cited gene set analysis (Liberzon et al., 2015).

claim: Clusters 2 and 5 expressed high levels of genes associated with a type I IFN response.
source: One major distinguishing characteristic between 'homeostatic' cluster 0 and 'infection' clusters 2 and 5 was the extent of ISG expression, in which cluster 0 expressed low levels of genes associated with a type I IFN response, even in infected animals, while clusters 2 and 5 expressed high levels of these genes (Figure 3D; Liberzon et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D and cited gene set analysis (Liberzon et al., 2015).

claim: The gene expression profile of clusters 2 and 5 was different between HSV-2 and HSV-1 infection at 5 d.p.i.
source: Furthermore, the gene expression profile of clusters 2 and 5 was different between HSV-2 and HSV-1 infection at 5 d.p.i. (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), including the expression of ISGs (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: IFNβ levels were higher in the vaginal lumen after HSV-2 infection compared to HSV-1 at time points corresponding to the onset of genital inflammation.
source: While type I IFN was robustly produced early during acute infection after both HSV-1 and HSV-2 infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), IFNβ levels were higher in the vaginal lumen after HSV-2 infection compared to HSV-1 at time points corresponding to the onset of genital inflammation (Figure 3E) despite similar viral burden between the two infection models (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Type I IFN was robustly produced early during acute infection after both HSV-1 and HSV-2 infection.
source: While type I IFN was robustly produced early during acute infection after both HSV-1 and HSV-2 infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), IFNβ levels were higher in the vaginal lumen after HSV-2 infection compared to HSV-1 at time points corresponding to the onset of genital inflammation (Figure 3E) despite similar viral burden between the two infection models (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: IFNβ was undetectable in both the vaginal lumen and the parenchyma by 7 days after both HSV-1 and HSV-2 infection.
source: IFNβ was undetectable in both the vaginal lumen and the parenchyma by 7 days after both HSV-1 and HSV-2 infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,C.

claim: When mice were injected i.p. with anti-IFNAR1 antibody on the day of HSV-2 inoculation, disease progression was more rapid compared to isotype control-treated animals.
source: When mice were injected i.p. with anti-IFNAR1 antibody on the day of HSV-2 inoculation, disease progression was more rapid compared to isotype control-treated animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), and the mice succumbed to infection at a faster rate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), in a manner similar to IFNAR1-deficient mice (Iversen et al., 2010; Iversen et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2017; Reinert et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by inflammation score data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mice treated with anti-IFNAR1 antibody on the day of HSV-2 inoculation succumbed to infection at a faster rate.
source: When mice were injected i.p. with anti-IFNAR1 antibody on the day of HSV-2 inoculation, disease progression was more rapid compared to isotype control-treated animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), and the mice succumbed to infection at a faster rate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), in a manner similar to IFNAR1-deficient mice (Iversen et al., 2010; Iversen et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2017; Reinert et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Inflammation and rapid disease progression after early anti-IFNAR1 treatment were likely due to significantly elevated viral burden in the anti-IFNAR1 antibody-treated mice compared to isotype controls.
source: Inflammation and rapid disease progression were likely due to significantly elevated viral burden in the anti-IFNAR1 antibody-treated mice compared to isotype controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), as HSV is a highly lytic virus that is capable of independently inducing epithelial tissue damage (Horbul et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and cited knowledge about HSV (Horbul et al., 2011).

claim: HSV is a highly lytic virus that is capable of independently inducing epithelial tissue damage.
source: Inflammation and rapid disease progression were likely due to significantly elevated viral burden in the anti-IFNAR1 antibody-treated mice compared to isotype controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), as HSV is a highly lytic virus that is capable of independently inducing epithelial tissue damage (Horbul et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Horbul et al., 2011.

claim: One treatment with therapeutic IFNAR1 blockade at 4 d.p.i. led to a significant reduction in the severity of inflammation compared to isotype controls.
source: In stark contrast to early anti-IFNAR1 antibody treatment, one treatment with therapeutic IFNAR1 blockade led to a significant reduction in the severity of inflammation compared to isotype controls (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by inflammation score data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: IFNAR1 blockade at 4 d.p.i. had little impact on mucosal viral shedding.
source: Furthermore, IFNAR1 blockade at 4 d.p.i. had little impact on mucosal viral shedding (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The protective effect of type I IFN on control of genital HSV infection is limited to the early stages of acute infection.
source: Collectively, these data show that the protective effect of type I IFN on control of genital HSV infection is limited to the early stages of acute infection, and that sustained IFN signaling in the later stages of acute HSV-2 genital infection drives inflammation with minimal effect on viral replication.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects of early vs late IFNAR1 blockade on disease and viral control.

claim: Sustained IFN signaling in the later stages of acute HSV-2 genital infection drives inflammation with minimal effect on viral replication.
source: Collectively, these data show that the protective effect of type I IFN on control of genital HSV infection is limited to the early stages of acute infection, and that sustained IFN signaling in the later stages of acute HSV-2 genital infection drives inflammation with minimal effect on viral replication.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing therapeutic IFNAR1 blockade reduces inflammation without affecting viral titers.

claim: The number of neutrophils recovered from the vaginal lumen was similar between the IFNAR1 CKO mice and their Cre- control littermates.
source: Despite differences in IFNAR1 expression, the number of neutrophils recovered from the vaginal lumen was similar between the IFNAR1 CKO mice and their Cre- control littermates (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The severity of genital inflammation presented by the IFNAR1 CKO mice was significantly reduced compared to the Cre- controls.
source: Strikingly, although the magnitude of the vaginal neutrophil response was similar, we found that the severity of genital inflammation presented by the IFNAR1 CKO mice was significantly reduced compared to the Cre- controls (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by inflammation score data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A subset of the IFNAR1 CKO cohort did not develop any signs of inflammation as late as 7 d.p.i.
source: As observed after neutrophil depletion, a subset of the IFNAR1 CKO cohort did not develop any signs of inflammation as late as 7 d.p.i. (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by inflammation score data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: IFNAR1 CKO mice exhibited less pathology in both the vagina and genital skin compared to Cre- controls.
source: Similar to our observations with therapeutic IFNAR1 blockade, IFNAR1 CKO mice exhibited less pathology in both the vagina and genital skin compared to Cre- controls (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Distinct disease outcomes between the Cre- controls and IFNAR1 CKO mice occurred independently of viral control.
source: Distinct disease outcomes between the Cre- controls and IFNAR1 CKO mice occurred independently of viral control, as viral loads in the mucosa were similar between the two groups (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Tissue inflammation during HSV-2 infection is largely driven by prolonged type I IFN production, which acts directly upon neutrophils to drive disease.
source: Together, our data demonstrates that tissue inflammation during HSV-2 infection is largely driven by prolonged type I IFN production, which acts directly upon neutrophils to drive disease.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined results of therapeutic IFNAR1 blockade and neutrophil-specific IFNAR1 deletion experiments.

claim: IL-18 levels were markedly reduced at 5 d.p.i. after therapeutic antibody-mediated IFNAR1 blockade.
source: At 5 d.p.i., similarly to neutrophil-depleted mice, we found that IL-18 levels were markedly reduced (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Measurement of IL-18 in the vagina of IFNAR1 CKO at 5 d.p.i. revealed a significant decrease in cytokine levels compared to littermate controls.
source: Importantly, measurement of IL-18 in the vagina of IFNAR1 CKO at 5 d.p.i. also revealed a significant decrease in cytokine levels compared to littermate controls (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Neutralization of IL-18 led to a considerable reduction in disease severity.
source: Remarkably, neutralization of IL-18 led to a considerable reduction in disease severity (Figure 6D), without any impact on viral control (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by inflammation score data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Neutralization of IL-18 had no impact on viral control.
source: Remarkably, neutralization of IL-18 led to a considerable reduction in disease severity (Figure 6D), without any impact on viral control (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Neutrophils could be a source of IL-18 during vaginal HSV-2 infection.
source: Detection of IL-18 and S100A8 around a single nucleus demonstrated that neutrophils could be a source of IL-18 during vaginal HSV-2 infection (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6F showing colocalization of IL-18 and S100A8.

claim: IL-18-reactive cells that were negative for S100A8 but in close proximity to neutrophils were identified, suggesting the potential for multiple cellular sources of IL-18.
source: However, we also identified IL-18-reactive cells that were negative for S100A8 but in close proximity to neutrophils (Figure 6F), suggesting the potential for multiple cellular sources of IL-18.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6F and represents an inference about multiple IL-18 sources.

claim: Sustained type I IFN signaling in neutrophils leads to the production of vaginal IL-18.
source: Thus, our data demonstrate that sustained type I IFN signaling in neutrophils leads to the production of vaginal IL-18 and reveal IL-18 to be a novel regulator of disease after HSV-2 infection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined results showing IFNAR1 blockade/deletion reduces IL-18 levels.

claim: IL-18 is a novel regulator of disease after HSV-2 infection.
source: Thus, our data demonstrate that sustained type I IFN signaling in neutrophils leads to the production of vaginal IL-18 and reveal IL-18 to be a novel regulator of disease after HSV-2 infection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing IL-18 neutralization reduces disease severity.

claim: Neutrophils promote genital inflammation without affecting antiviral activity after genital HSV-2 infection.
source: We found that neutrophils promote genital inflammation without affecting antiviral activity after genital HSV-2 infection, suggesting that the neutrophil response is primarily immunopathogenic.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing neutrophil depletion reduces inflammation without affecting viral titers.

claim: The neutrophil response is primarily immunopathogenic during HSV-2 infection.
source: We found that neutrophils promote genital inflammation without affecting antiviral activity after genital HSV-2 infection, suggesting that the neutrophil response is primarily immunopathogenic.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing neutrophils drive disease without contributing to viral control.

claim: Depletion of neutrophils led to a significant decrease in disease severity without altering recruitment of other immune cells.
source: Depletion of neutrophils led to a significant decrease in disease severity without altering recruitment of other immune cells or the production of common pro-inflammatory cytokines, and deficiency in genes controlling neutrophil effector functions such as ROS production and NET formation had little impact on progression of disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by inflammation score data and flow cytometry data showing no changes in other immune cell populations after neutrophil depletion.

claim: Depletion of neutrophils did not alter the production of common pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: Depletion of neutrophils led to a significant decrease in disease severity without altering recruitment of other immune cells or the production of common pro-inflammatory cytokines, and deficiency in genes controlling neutrophil effector functions such as ROS production and NET formation had little impact on progression of disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deficiency in genes controlling neutrophil effector functions such as ROS production and NET formation had little impact on progression of disease.
source: Depletion of neutrophils led to a significant decrease in disease severity without altering recruitment of other immune cells or the production of common pro-inflammatory cytokines, and deficiency in genes controlling neutrophil effector functions such as ROS production and NET formation had little impact on progression of disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by inflammation score and viral titer data from PAD4 CKO, Ncf2 KO, and STIM1/2 DKO mice.

claim: Host responses to HSV-1 and HSV-2 established distinct inflammatory milieus with divergent effects on responding neutrophils.
source: Comparative analysis of single-cell transcriptional profiles revealed a strong type I IFN signature that was sustained in neutrophils responding to a highly inflammatory genital HSV-2 infection but not a less inflammatory HSV-1 infection, suggesting that host responses to these two related viruses established distinct inflammatory milieus with divergent effects on responding neutrophils.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the scRNA-seq data showing differential ISG expression in neutrophils after HSV-1 vs HSV-2 infection.

claim: Antibody-mediated blockade of IFNAR1 at the time of infection led to significantly worse disease outcomes.
source: In contrast to antibody-mediated blockade of IFNAR1 at the time of infection, which led to significantly worse disease outcomes, IFNAR1 blockade just prior to the resolution phase of acute mucosal infection significantly delayed the progression of genital inflammation.
evidence: This claim is supported by inflammation score and survival data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: IFNAR1 blockade just prior to the resolution phase of acute mucosal infection significantly delayed the progression of genital inflammation.
source: In contrast to antibody-mediated blockade of IFNAR1 at the time of infection, which led to significantly worse disease outcomes, IFNAR1 blockade just prior to the resolution phase of acute mucosal infection significantly delayed the progression of genital inflammation.
evidence: This claim is supported by inflammation score data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Neutrophil-specific deficiency of IFNAR1 markedly reduced the severity of genital disease after HSV-2 infection.
source: Importantly, neutrophil-specific deficiency of IFNAR1 markedly reduced the severity of genital disease after HSV-2 infection, suggesting that persistent IFN signaling drove disease primarily by acting on neutrophils.
evidence: This claim is supported by inflammation score data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Persistent IFN signaling drove disease primarily by acting on neutrophils.
source: Importantly, neutrophil-specific deficiency of IFNAR1 markedly reduced the severity of genital disease after HSV-2 infection, suggesting that persistent IFN signaling drove disease primarily by acting on neutrophils.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing neutrophil-specific IFNAR1 deletion reduces disease severity.

claim: Sustained type I IFN signaling is a key factor in distinguishing between pathogenic and non-pathogenic neutrophil responses during mucosal viral infection.
source: Together, our results suggest an axis of type I IFNs, neutrophils, and IL-18 as the key driver of genital disease in a mouse model of HSV-2 infection, and that sustained type I IFN signaling is a key factor in distinguishing between pathogenic and non-pathogenic neutrophil responses during mucosal viral infection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined experimental results comparing HSV-1 and HSV-2 infections and the effects of IFNAR1 manipulation.

claim: An axis of type I IFNs, neutrophils, and IL-18 is the key driver of genital disease in a mouse model of HSV-2 infection.
source: Together, our results suggest an axis of type I IFNs, neutrophils, and IL-18 as the key driver of genital disease in a mouse model of HSV-2 infection, and that sustained type I IFN signaling is a key factor in distinguishing between pathogenic and non-pathogenic neutrophil responses during mucosal viral infection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined experimental results showing the interconnected roles of type I IFN, neutrophils, and IL-18 in driving disease.

claim: Models of chronic viral infection reveal the detrimental effect of overexuberant or sustained type I IFN signaling.
source: Type I IFNs are a frontline of defense against viral infection, but models of chronic viral infection, including lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) (Teijaro et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2013), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) (Meier et al., 2009; Rotger et al., 2010; Sedaghat et al., 2008; Taleb et al., 2017), and simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) (Harris et al., 2010; Jacquelin et al., 2009), reveal the detrimental effect of overexuberant or sustained type I IFN signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on chronic viral infections.

claim: Prolonged IFN signaling during chronic viral infection can promote immunosuppression through multiple cellular and molecular mechanisms.
source: Notably, prolonged IFN signaling during chronic viral infection can promote immunosuppression through multiple cellular and molecular mechanisms, and deletion or blockade of IFNAR1 during chronic LCMV infection can alleviate immunosuppression and enhance long-term viral control (Cheng et al., 2017; Taleb et al., 2017; Teijaro et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Cheng et al., 2017; Taleb et al., 2017; Teijaro et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2013).

claim: Deletion or blockade of IFNAR1 during chronic LCMV infection can alleviate immunosuppression and enhance long-term viral control.
source: Notably, prolonged IFN signaling during chronic viral infection can promote immunosuppression through multiple cellular and molecular mechanisms, and deletion or blockade of IFNAR1 during chronic LCMV infection can alleviate immunosuppression and enhance long-term viral control (Cheng et al., 2017; Taleb et al., 2017; Teijaro et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Cheng et al., 2017; Taleb et al., 2017; Teijaro et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2013).

claim: Early blockade of type I IFN signaling led to more severe disease and a complete loss of viral control after HSV-2 infection.
source: However, unlike the LCMV model, early blockade of type I IFN signaling led to more severe disease and a complete loss of viral control after HSV-2 infection, similar to infections performed on an IFNAR1-deficient genetic background (Iversen et al., 2010; Iversen et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2017; Leib et al., 1999; Reinert et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012), indicating an early antiviral role (Lee et al., 2017; Luker et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Only therapeutic inhibition of sustained IFN signaling diminished disease without disrupting viral control.
source: Rather, only therapeutic inhibition of sustained IFN signaling diminished disease without disrupting viral control, thus revealing a heretofore unappreciated, temporal division of the antiviral and immunopathological effects of type I IFN signaling during HSV-2 infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing differential effects of early vs late IFNAR1 blockade.

claim: There is a temporal division of the antiviral and immunopathological effects of type I IFN signaling during HSV-2 infection.
source: Rather, only therapeutic inhibition of sustained IFN signaling diminished disease without disrupting viral control, thus revealing a heretofore unappreciated, temporal division of the antiviral and immunopathological effects of type I IFN signaling during HSV-2 infection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing differential effects of early vs late IFNAR1 blockade.

claim: The source of sustained type I IFN production that promotes immunopathology after genital HSV-2 infection is currently unknown.
source: The source of sustained type I IFN production that promotes immunopathology after genital HSV-2 infection is currently unknown.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of a knowledge gap identified by the authors.

claim: It is unclear as to why type I IFN production is sustained during HSV-2, but not after genital HSV-1 infection.
source: It is also unclear as to why type I IFN production is sustained during HSV-2, but not after genital HSV-1 infection.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of a knowledge gap identified by the authors.

claim: Differences in viral dissemination to the nervous system or function of viral proteins may account for disparities in type I IFN production and ultimately, disease severity.
source: Differences in viral dissemination to the nervous system (Lee et al., 2020) or function of viral proteins may account for disparities in type I IFN production and ultimately, disease severity.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms, with one aspect supported by a citation (Lee et al., 2020).

claim: HSV encodes numerous proteins that can suppress type I IFN production and regulate the signaling pathways.
source: HSV encodes numerous proteins that can suppress type I IFN production and regulate the signaling pathways (Christensen et al., 2016; Lin and Zheng, 2019; Melroe et al., 2004), suggesting that production of type I IFN likely occurs from a cell type that is not directly infected.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Christensen et al., 2016; Lin and Zheng, 2019; Melroe et al., 2004).

claim: Production of type I IFN likely occurs from a cell type that is not directly infected with HSV.
source: HSV encodes numerous proteins that can suppress type I IFN production and regulate the signaling pathways (Christensen et al., 2016; Lin and Zheng, 2019; Melroe et al., 2004), suggesting that production of type I IFN likely occurs from a cell type that is not directly infected.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited knowledge about HSV's ability to suppress IFN production.

claim: Plasmacytoid dendritic cells appear to have a limited role during genital HSV-2 infection.
source: While plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDC) are known as robust producers of type I IFN, they appear to have a limited role during genital HSV-2 infection (Swiecki et al., 2013), indicating an alternative source of type I IFN, such as conventional DCs (Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Swiecki et al., 2013.

claim: Type I IFN can be detected at active lesion sites during recurrent episodes in humans.
source: In humans, type I IFN can be detected at active lesion sites during recurrent episodes (Peng et al., 2009; Roychoudhury et al., 2020), although levels do not correlate with restriction of viral replication (Roychoudhury et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Peng et al., 2009; Roychoudhury et al., 2020).

claim: Type I IFN levels do not correlate with restriction of viral replication during recurrent episodes in humans.
source: In humans, type I IFN can be detected at active lesion sites during recurrent episodes (Peng et al., 2009; Roychoudhury et al., 2020), although levels do not correlate with restriction of viral replication (Roychoudhury et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Roychoudhury et al., 2020.

claim: Type I IFN induction may not be antiviral and could contribute to ulcer formation in humans.
source: This raises the possibility that type I IFN induction may not be antiviral and could contribute to ulcer formation, although this hypothesis is yet to be tested.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential mechanism that has not been tested.

claim: Human neutrophils from females are reported to be hyper-responsive to type I IFNs.
source: Human neutrophils from females are also reported to be hyper-responsive to type I IFNs (Gupta et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gupta et al., 2020.

claim: Clinical disease recurrence rates between men and women with genital herpes are similar.
source: Although clinical disease recurrence rates between men and women with genital herpes are similar (Wald et al., 2002), differences in neutrophil sensitivity to type I IFN may have implications for sex-dependent mechanisms of ulcer development.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wald et al., 2002.

claim: Differences in neutrophil sensitivity to type I IFN may have implications for sex-dependent mechanisms of ulcer development.
source: Although clinical disease recurrence rates between men and women with genital herpes are similar (Wald et al., 2002), differences in neutrophil sensitivity to type I IFN may have implications for sex-dependent mechanisms of ulcer development.
evidence: This is speculation about potential implications of sex differences in neutrophil IFN responsiveness.

claim: Synergistic effects of cytokine signaling have been reported to be important for maximizing cellular responses to infection.
source: Synergistic effects of cytokine signaling have been reported to be important for maximizing cellular responses to infection through the upregulation of cooperative or independent molecular programs (Bartee and McFadden, 2013) or through the cross-regulation of receptor signaling pathways (Ivashkiv and Donlin, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Bartee and McFadden, 2013; Ivashkiv and Donlin, 2014).

claim: Type I, type II, and type III IFNs are all robustly produced during HSV-2 infection.
source: Upon infection, the activity of neutrophils can be modulated strongly by multiple IFNs, in a variety of tissues. Type I (Ank et al., 2008), type II (Iijima et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2020), and type III IFNs (Ank et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2020) are all robustly produced during HSV-2 infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Ank et al., 2008; Iijima et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2020).

claim: Type I and type II IFNs are crucial for the control of HSV-2 replication.
source: While type I and type II IFNs are crucial for the control of HSV-2 replication, endogenous type III IFNs do not appear to affect either disease severity or viral control, although exogenous application of type III IFNs can reduce viral burden (Ank et al., 2008; Ank et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations (Ank et al., 2008; Ank et al., 2006).

claim: Endogenous type III IFNs do not appear to affect either disease severity or viral control during HSV-2 infection.
source: While type I and type II IFNs are crucial for the control of HSV-2 replication, endogenous type III IFNs do not appear to affect either disease severity or viral control, although exogenous application of type III IFNs can reduce viral burden (Ank et al., 2008; Ank et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Ank et al., 2008; Ank et al., 2006).

claim: Exogenous application of type III IFNs can reduce viral burden during HSV-2 infection.
source: While type I and type II IFNs are crucial for the control of HSV-2 replication, endogenous type III IFNs do not appear to affect either disease severity or viral control, although exogenous application of type III IFNs can reduce viral burden (Ank et al., 2008; Ank et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Ank et al., 2008; Ank et al., 2006).

claim: Expression of the type III IFN receptor, IFNLR, is limited to very few cell types, including neutrophils and epithelial cells.
source: Expression of the type III IFN receptor, IFNLR, is limited to very few cell types, including neutrophils and epithelial cells (Blazek et al., 2015; Mahlakõiv et al., 2015; Sommereyns et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Blazek et al., 2015; Mahlakõiv et al., 2015; Sommereyns et al., 2008).

claim: In vitro stimulation of neutrophils with type I IFN leads to the upregulation of many common ISGs as well as inflammatory genes, including IL-18.
source: In vitro stimulation of neutrophils with type I IFN leads to the upregulation of many common ISGs as well as inflammatory genes, including IL-18 (Galani et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Galani et al., 2017.

claim: Type I IFN may differentially regulate expression of IL-18 and IL-1β.
source: Importantly, type I IFN may differentially regulate expression of IL-18 and IL-1β, another IL-1 family cytokine that depends on caspase-mediated cleavage for activation (Zhu and Kanneganti, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhu and Kanneganti, 2017.

claim: It is unclear whether neutrophils are directly producing IL-18 in the HSV-2 infection model.
source: It is unclear whether neutrophils are directly producing this cytokine in our model of infection and whether IL-18 production is dependent on inflammasome activation.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of a knowledge gap identified by the authors.

claim: It is unclear whether IL-18 production is dependent on inflammasome activation in the HSV-2 infection model.
source: It is unclear whether neutrophils are directly producing this cytokine in our model of infection and whether IL-18 production is dependent on inflammasome activation.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of a knowledge gap identified by the authors.

claim: HSV encodes proteins that can inhibit inflammasome activity.
source: As HSV also encodes proteins that can inhibit inflammasome activity (Maruzuru et al., 2018), one possibility is that IL-18 is produced by a cell type that is not productively infected with HSV, such as neutrophils.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Maruzuru et al., 2018.

claim: IL-18 may be produced by a cell type that is not productively infected with HSV, such as neutrophils.
source: As HSV also encodes proteins that can inhibit inflammasome activity (Maruzuru et al., 2018), one possibility is that IL-18 is produced by a cell type that is not productively infected with HSV, such as neutrophils.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential mechanism for IL-18 production.

claim: Neutrophil proteases released in the extracellular space have been reported to cleave and activate proIL-1 cytokines that are secreted by other cells in a caspase-1-independent manner.
source: Alternatively, neutrophil proteases released in the extracellular space have been reported to cleave and activate proIL-1 cytokines that are secreted by other cells in a caspase-1-independent manner (Clancy et al., 2018; Robertson et al., 2006; Sugawara et al., 2001), suggesting a mechanism by which neutrophils may modulate IL-18 levels without directly secreting the cytokine themselves.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Clancy et al., 2018; Robertson et al., 2006; Sugawara et al., 2001).

claim: During HSV-2 vaginal infection, IL-18 stimulates NK cells to rapidly produce antiviral IFNγ.
source: During HSV-2 vaginal infection, IL-18 stimulates NK cells to rapidly produce antiviral IFNγ (Lee et al., 2017), and is thought to be important for orchestrating a protective innate immune response.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2017.

claim: IL-18-deficient mice are more susceptible to HSV-2 infection.
source: Accordingly, IL-18-deficient mice are more susceptible to HSV-2 infection (Harandi et al., 2001) and HSV-1 infection (Fujioka et al., 1999; Reading et al., 2007), presumably due to dysregulation of innate IFNγ production and loss of viral control.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Harandi et al., 2001; Fujioka et al., 1999; Reading et al., 2007).

claim: IL-18-deficient mice are more susceptible to HSV-1 infection.
source: Accordingly, IL-18-deficient mice are more susceptible to HSV-2 infection (Harandi et al., 2001) and HSV-1 infection (Fujioka et al., 1999; Reading et al., 2007), presumably due to dysregulation of innate IFNγ production and loss of viral control.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Fujioka et al., 1999; Reading et al., 2007).

claim: There may be a temporal component to the effects of IL-18 during HSV-2 infection.
source: Our study reveals a novel aspect of IL-18 biology during HSV-2 infection, and that like type I IFN signaling, there may be a temporal component to the effects of IL-18 during HSV-2 infection.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed dual roles of IL-18 in protection and pathology.

claim: The mechanism by which IL-18 promotes disease during genital HSV-2 infection is currently unknown.
source: Currently, the mechanism by which IL-18 promotes disease during genital HSV-2 infection is unknown.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of a knowledge gap identified by the authors.

claim: In the gut, the role of IL-18 is balanced between protection and pathology.
source: In the gut, the role of IL-18 is balanced between protection and pathology (Jarret et al., 2020; Nowarski et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Jarret et al., 2020; Nowarski et al., 2015).

claim: The role of IL-18 during HSV-2 infection appears to be complex.
source: The role of IL-18 during HSV-2 infection appears to be similarly complex, and further study will be required to identify the compartment on which IL-18 acts and the downstream effects of IL-18 signaling.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed dual roles of IL-18 in protection and pathology.

claim: The reduction in disease severity after IL-18 neutralization was not as profound as therapeutic IFNAR blockade.
source: Additionally, while our results demonstrate an important role for IL-18, the reduction in disease severity was not as profound as therapeutic IFNAR blockade in our HSV-2 model of infection.
evidence: This is an observation comparing the effects of IL-18 neutralization and IFNAR blockade on disease severity.

claim: Other IL-18-independent, IFN-dependent mechanisms that promote genital inflammation are yet to be elucidated.
source: Considering the complex response elicited by type I IFN, our data suggest that other IL-18-independent, IFN-dependent mechanisms that promote genital inflammation are yet to be elucidated.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that IL-18 neutralization does not fully recapitulate the effects of IFNAR blockade.

claim: Therapeutic neutralization of IL-18 reduced disease without altering viral titers.
source: Nevertheless, therapeutic neutralization of IL-18 reduced disease without altering viral titers in our model, suggesting that IL-18 does not have an impact on T-cell-dependent IFNγ production (Milligan and Bernstein, 1997; Nakanishi et al., 2009) or direct antiviral activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6D and 6E.

claim: IL-18 does not have an impact on T-cell-dependent IFNγ production during HSV-2 infection.
source: Nevertheless, therapeutic neutralization of IL-18 reduced disease without altering viral titers in our model, suggesting that IL-18 does not have an impact on T-cell-dependent IFNγ production (Milligan and Bernstein, 1997; Nakanishi et al., 2009) or direct antiviral activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that IL-18 neutralization does not affect viral control, supported by citations (Milligan and Bernstein, 1997; Nakanishi et al., 2009).

claim: IL-18 is dispensable for stimulating IFNγ from adaptive memory immune responses.
source: As previous studies have shown that IL-18 is also dispensable for stimulating IFNγ from adaptive memory immune responses (Harandi et al., 2001), IL-18, along with type I IFN, may present attractive targets for therapeutics aiming to reduce inflammation during genital herpes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harandi et al., 2001.

claim: IL-18, along with type I IFN, may present attractive targets for therapeutics aiming to reduce inflammation during genital herpes.
source: As previous studies have shown that IL-18 is also dispensable for stimulating IFNγ from adaptive memory immune responses (Harandi et al., 2001), IL-18, along with type I IFN, may present attractive targets for therapeutics aiming to reduce inflammation during genital herpes.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic applications based on the experimental findings.
